title: Render to Caesar (Mark 11:27–12:17)
hookLine: a coin with Caesar's image; what bears God's image belongs to God

lines: A QUESTION WITH NO SAFE ANSWER.
PAY TAXES TO CAESAR, OR NOT?
cards: The question with no safe answer: the one at a family dinner that's really a trap, where whichever way you answer, somebody's furious. Jesus walks the Temple courts, and the questions start.
By what authority do you do these things? He answers with a question of his own, and tells a story about tenants who kill the owner's son.
Then a group arrives with the perfect trap, some Pharisees, some supporters of Herod. They flatter him first. Then: should we pay taxes to Caesar, or not?

teach.h: A TRAP WITH NO SAFE ANSWER.
teach.b: First, the trap. Say yes, pay, and he sides with Rome, the occupier, and the crowd turns on him. Say no, and he's a rebel, and Rome has a cross for rebels.
Second, the coin. Bring me a penny, he says, let me see it: a Roman denarius, the tax coin.

teach.h: WHOSE IMAGE IS ON THE COIN?
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "Whose is this image and inscription?" Caesar's. The emperor's face is on it, and around the edge, words calling him the son of a god.
Notice: he has to ask them for one, and they can produce it, there in the Temple courts. Third, the answer: render "to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's."
Mark says they marveled at him. It's not a dodge; it has a hook in it.
The coin has Caesar's image, so give it back.
Then what has God's image on it? Anyone who knew the first page of Genesis would hear it: "And God created man to his own image: to the image of God he created him."

teach.h: AND TO GOD THE THINGS THAT ARE GOD'S.
teach.b: Early Christian writers loved this: the coin carries Caesar's face, and you carry God's. Fourth, what this means for Catholics now.
The Church teaches that Christians owe real duties to their country: pay taxes, vote, serve the common good. But the state doesn't own the whole person. The deepest part, the image, belongs to God.
So the line both honors earthly duty and sets a limit on it. Your wallet can go to Caesar. You can't.

how: The Catholic Church teaches that citizens have duties to the state, such as paying taxes and voting, and that every human being is made in the image of God, which grounds its teaching on human dignity.

games.q: you're Jesus in the Temple. yes, pay the tax: the crowd turns on you. no, don't pay: Rome arrests you. what do you do?
o: say yes, and lose the crowd.
ask for a coin, and ask whose image is on it.
games.why: "Whose is this image and inscription?" "Caesar's." then: to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's.

practice: Look at your face in a mirror or your phone's camera, or picture it if neither is near, and skip the usual checklist: hair, skin, tired eyes.

Look the way you'd look at a coin to see whose image it bears; Catholics say that face was made in the image of God. If you pray, you can give thanks for it; if you don't, just let yourself be looked at kindly, even by yourself.

wordCard.voice: Image. The word on the coin, and the word Genesis uses for how God made us: Caesar's face on the coin, God's on you. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: image, the word on the coin, and the word the Greek Bible uses for the image of God in Genesis. icon comes from it.

carryVoice: Your line: you bear his image. So, it's said, does every face you pass. That's day two hundred twenty-two.
